channel.title: The Year — The Earthly Book of Hours
channel.description: The year a day at a time, as kept in the Boston Basin: a subject of the season each day, with an image and a reading, and each week its Lectio Terra essay. It comes round again every year.

item.title: 26 November: Wild Turkey
item.description:
James McNeill Whistler, Turkeys, a Venice courtyard etched in 1880 and published in the “Second Venice Set” (1886). When the edition was complete, the copper was scored with crossed lines so no more could be printed, and this proof was pulled to show that it was finished.

I am, on this account, not displeas’d that the Figure is not known as a Bald Eagle, but looks more like a Turk’y. For in Truth, the Turk’y is in comparison a much more respectable Bird, and withal a true original Native of America. Eagles have been found in all Countries, but the Turk’y was peculiar to ours; the first of the Species seen in Europe being brought to France by the Jesuits from Canada, and serv’d up at the Wedding Table of Charles the Ninth. He is, [though a little vain and silly, it is true, but not the worse emblem for that,] a Bird of Courage, and would not hesitate to attack a Grenadier of the British Guards, who should presume to invade his Farm Yard with a red Coat on.

Benjamin Franklin, from a letter to Sarah Bache (Passy, 26 January 1784)

item.title: 25 November: The Three Sisters
item.description:
A Seneca youth, the march of the Toñwiʹsas, the women’s society of the three sisters, pen drawing printed as figure 2 in Arthur C. Parker, Iroquois Uses of Maize and Other Food Plants (1910), p. 28 (printed sideways on the page)

The corn was carefully dropped in the hills so as not to break the germs which had nearly burst through. Among the Senecas, in planting corn the seeds of the squash and bean were sown in every seventh hill because it was thought that the spirits of these three plants were inseparable. They were called Dioʹhe″ko, these sustain us. In the Green Corn Thanksgiving the leader rises and says, “Diettinoⁿʹñioʻ diohe″koⁿ, we give thanks to our sustainers.”

Certain women banded themselves together in a society called the Toñwisas or Toⁿwiʹsas Oäʹno. They propitiated the spirits of the three sisters by certain ceremonies. In their ceremonial march, Wenŭntoñwiʹsăs, the leader holding an armful of corn and a cake of corn bread leads her band in a measured march about a kettle of corn soup.

Arthur C. Parker, from Iroquois Uses of Maize and Other Food Plants (1910), p. 27

item.title: 24 November: Hubbard Squash
item.description:
James J. H. Gregory, “Section of Squash-House,” from Squashes: How to Grow Them (1867), p. 34, wood engraving

In handling the squashes, I need hardly reiterate the caution of care. My practice is to form a string of boys, from the wagon to the shelves, and the squashes are tossed from one to another, with the caution to handle them like eggs. Boys well trained will not drop more than one squash to the ton, and I have known my boys to pass several tons without dropping a single squash.

If the squash-house has been built with reference to warmth, when once filled with squashes, it is surprising with what little fire frost can be kept out. The mass of squashes are, in themselves, a great store-house of heat, and with inside shutters for the coldest weather, the building is frost proof, with a small outlay of fuel.

James J. H. Gregory, “The Storing of the Crop,” from Squashes: How to Grow Them (1867), pp. 35–36

item.title: 23 November: American Chestnut
item.description:
Mary Vaux Walcott, American Chestnut (Castanea dentata) (1932), watercolour

NOW-A-DAYS one often hears the question, “What is going to become of our chestnut trees?” In fact, whenever the subject of trees is broached in the course of a conversation, this inquiry is bound to come out—not, as I believe, that the interrogator hopes to receive a satisfactory answer, but more in the way of a general query.

Arthur H. Graves, “The Future of the Chestnut Tree in North America”, Popular Science Monthly 84 (June 1914), p. 551

item.title: Lectio Terra: Fen and Wetland
item.description:
Charles Kingsley, Amy Lowell, Arielle Kaplan, John Clare

While fall may be the season of the woodlands, the transition into winter can shift plant and animal activity toward the lower, tighter structure of all those water-adjacent landforms: fens, marshlands, bogs, mires and quagmires, swamps, sloughs, and swales—not to mention bayous, pocosins, and the many other regional variations of wetlands. If you’ve never stopped to wonder how these terms relate…

item.title: Lectio Terra: Eastern Grey Squirrel
item.description:
Meriwether Lewis, John Burroughs, Ralph Waldo Emerson

My brother called them “joeys” and “jojos” as a child, for reasons that escape me. Maybe he was thinking of young marsupials or mispronouncing the word “chipmunk.” At any rate, squirrels were one of the first forms of wildlife detectable through our family’s windows, in our backyard, or at the playgrounds we frequented. Like many suburban households, our closest neighbors were likely not people…
